title: Insects and small creatures: counting legs, and how a tiny ant carries so much

summary.text: An ant can carry off a crumb bigger than her own head. Ants, bees and butterflies are insects: they have six legs, three body parts and two feelers. A spider has eight legs and two body parts, so a spider is not an insect. An earthworm has no legs at all. Your child counts legs, then puts biscuit crumbs of four sizes beside an ant line and watches which ones the ants carry home.
summary.art: A tiny black ant on a kitchen floor carrying a white biscuit crumb bigger than her head, with a spider in the corner and a butterfly at the window.

intro.hook: A crumb is moving across the kitchen floor by itself. Look closer. An ant is carrying the crumb. How can something so small carry so much?
intro.text: Small creatures live all around us, even in a flat. Ants walk in lines in the kitchen. A spider waits in a corner of the bathroom. A butterfly visits the curry leaf plant on the balcony. Some of these small creatures are insects, and some are not. You can tell them apart by counting their legs. In this unit you count legs on ants, spiders and butterflies. Then you test how big a crumb an ant can carry.
intro.art: A city kitchen floor with a line of ants, one ant carrying a crumb, and a child crouching with a magnifying glass.

outcomes: By the end I can say that an insect has six legs, three body parts and two feelers, and name some insects: ants, bees and butterflies.
By the end I can say why a spider is not an insect: a spider has eight legs and two body parts.
By the end I can say that an earthworm has no legs, and moves with muscles and tiny bristles.
By the end I can count the legs on a small creature, or on a picture, and sort small creatures by their legs.
By the end I can make a guess with a reason, test which crumbs ants carry, count what is left and say what I found.
By the end I can say that small animals are very strong for their size, and that ants, bees, spiders and worms sense the world and make choices.

terms.meaning: An insect is a small animal with six legs and a body in three parts: the head, the middle and the back part.
terms.example: Ants, bees, butterflies, mosquitoes and cockroaches are all insects. Each one has six legs.
terms.art: An ant, a honeybee and a butterfly side by side, each with their six legs drawn clearly.

terms.meaning: Antennae are the two feelers on an insect's head. Insects use them to smell and to touch.
terms.example: When two ants meet, they tap each other with their antennae. That is how they smell who the other ant is.
terms.art: Two ants face to face, touching each other's antennae.

terms.meaning: The thorax is the middle part of an insect's body. All six legs grow from the thorax, and so do the wings.
terms.example: Look at a bee. Her legs and her wings all join on to her middle part, the thorax.
terms.art: A large drawing of a bee with the head, the thorax and the back part coloured differently, and arrows showing the legs joining the thorax.

terms.meaning: The abdomen is the back part of an insect's body. Food is digested there.
terms.example: A honeybee's abdomen has yellow and black stripes. Her sting is at the tip of her abdomen.
terms.art: A honeybee from the side with her striped abdomen labelled.

terms.meaning: A spider is a small animal with eight legs and a body in two parts. Spiders are not insects.
terms.example: The thin-legged spider in the bathroom corner has eight legs. Count them: four on each side.
terms.art: A spider with eight long thin legs in the corner of a bathroom ceiling, with four legs on each side numbered.

terms.meaning: Silk is a strong, thin thread that some animals make inside their bodies. Spiders make silk, and so do silkworms.
terms.example: A spider's web is made of silk. A Kanchipuram silk saree is made from the silk of silkworms.
terms.art: A round spider web with dew drops on the threads, and beside it a folded silk saree.

terms.meaning: An earthworm is a long, soft animal with no legs, whose body is made of many rings. Earthworms live in damp soil.
terms.example: After the first rain of the monsoon, earthworms often come up out of the soil onto the path.
terms.art: A pink-brown earthworm on damp soil, with the rings of the body showing.

terms.meaning: A colony is a big family of animals who live together and share the work. Ants and honeybees live in colonies.
terms.example: One ant colony can have thousands of ants. Almost all of them are sisters, and one or more queens lay the eggs.
terms.art: A cut-away view of an ant nest under the ground, with tunnels, rooms, eggs and many ants.

explanations.context: This card is about how to tell that a small creature is an insect.
explanations.definition: An insect has six legs, a body in three parts (head, thorax and abdomen) and two antennae. Most insects also have wings.
explanations.description: Count the legs first. Every grown-up insect has six legs, three on each side, and all six join the middle part, the thorax. On the head are two antennae, which smell and touch. Many insects have wings: a bee has four, and a housefly has two. Some butterflies seem to have only four legs, but the front two are tiny and folded up under the head. So they still have six.
examples: An ant: six legs, three body parts, two antennae, and no wings on most ants.
A honeybee: six legs, four wings, two antennae.
A butterfly: six legs, four big wings, two antennae with a little knob at the tip.
A cockroach and a mosquito are insects too.
explanations.art: A big labelled drawing of an ant: head with two antennae, thorax with six legs, and abdomen.

explanations.concept: A spider is not an insect
explanations.context: This card is about why a spider is not an insect, even though both are small and have many legs.
explanations.definition: A spider has eight legs, a body in two parts and no antennae. Insects have six legs, three body parts and two antennae.
explanations.description: Count a spider's legs and you get eight, four on each side. A spider's body has two parts: a front part with the legs, eyes and mouth, and a round back part. Spiders have no antennae and no wings. Some spiders build webs of silk to catch insects. Others, like the small jumping spiders on our walls, have no web. They creep up and jump on their food. Spiders, scorpions and ticks are all arachnids, and all have eight legs.
examples: The thin-legged spider in a bathroom corner: eight legs, two body parts.
A jumping spider on a window frame: eight legs and two very big front eyes.
A scorpion: eight legs, so a scorpion is in the spider group too.
explanations.art: An ant and a spider side by side, the same size, with their legs numbered: 6 on the ant and 8 on the spider, and their body parts outlined.

explanations.context: This card is about how an earthworm moves without any legs.
explanations.definition: An earthworm has no legs. Muscles squeeze and stretch the body, and tiny bristles grip the soil.
explanations.description: An earthworm's body is made of many rings, with muscles under the skin. First the front end gets long and thin and pushes forward. Then the body gets short and fat, and pulls the back end along. On each ring there are tiny stiff hairs called bristles. They grip the soil so the worm does not slide back. Earthworms breathe through their skin, so the skin must stay damp.
examples: Earthworms in the soil of a big potted plant.
Earthworms on a wet path after the first monsoon rain.
Earthworms in a vermicompost bin, turning vegetable peels into soil.
explanations.art: Three drawings of one earthworm moving: front end stretched long and thin, then the body short and fat, then stretched again further along.

explanations.concept: Small bodies are strong for their size
explanations.context: This card explains why an ant can carry such a big crumb. Read it after the crumb test.
explanations.definition: A small animal can carry a much bigger load, for the size of their body, than a big animal can.
explanations.description: Many ants can carry things heavier than their own bodies. A person cannot carry a load as heavy as a car. Here is why size matters. A muscle's strength depends on how thick it is, and a body's weight depends on how much of it there is. Imagine an ant made twice as long, twice as wide and twice as tall. Her muscles would be about 4 times as strong, but her body would be about 8 times as heavy. So a small body is very light for the strength of its muscles, and ants can carry so much.
examples: An ant carrying a sugar grain bigger than her own head.
A group of ants dragging a crumb too big for one ant.
A person can carry a school bag, but not a load as big as the person.
explanations.art: On the left, an ant holding up a crumb bigger than her head. On the right, a girl trying to lift a sofa as big as herself, and not managing.

explanations.context: This card is about the minds of small creatures, and what scientists still argue about.
explanations.description: Ants, bees, spiders and worms sense the world, remember and make choices. A honeybee learns which flower colours give her food, and remembers the way back. She then dances in the hive to tell her sisters where the flowers are. A jumping spider watches her food, then plans a path to creep up on it. Scientists agree about what these animals do. They still argue about what, if anything, the animals feel while they do it.
examples: A honeybee dances to show her sisters where the flowers are.
Ants call more ants to a big crumb.
In a 2022 test, bumblebees rolled small balls again and again, with no food as a reward.

perspectives.who: Hiruni Samadi Galpayage Dona, a scientist from Sri Lanka working in London, and her team
perspectives.explanation: In 2022 they gave bumblebees small wooden balls. Many bees rolled the balls again and again, though there was no food for it. Young bees rolled them most. The team said this looks like play, and that insects may have good and bad feelings.

perspectives.who: Many other scientists who study insects
perspectives.explanation: We can see what insects do, but not what they feel. Many of their actions are built into their bodies from birth. We should be careful before saying that an insect enjoys something the way a child does.

explanations.art: A fuzzy bumblebee pushing a small yellow ball across a floor, with two more bees watching.

agreed.text: Every grown-up insect has six legs, a body in three parts and two antennae.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have described about a million kinds of insects. Ants, bees, butterflies, beetles, flies and all the rest have six legs as grown-ups.

agreed.text: Spiders have eight legs and two body parts, so spiders are not insects.
agreed.evidence: Every kind of spider ever found has eight legs. Their bodies, eyes and silk are built differently from any insect's.

agreed.text: Small animals are much stronger for their size than big animals.
agreed.evidence: In 1638 Galileo, an Italian scientist, worked out that when a body grows, the weight grows faster than the strength. Scientists who weigh ants and their loads find many ants carry loads heavier than themselves.

challenging.who: A very common idea. Even Carl Linnaeus, a famous Swedish scientist, put spiders in his group of insects in 1758.
challenging.for: Spiders are small, have many legs and no bones, and live in the same places as insects.
challenging.against: Count the legs: a spider has eight, an insect has six. A spider has two body parts, not three, and no antennae. Scientists later moved spiders into their own group, with scorpions and ticks.
challenging.context: This card is about a mix-up that even scientists once made.

challenging.claim: If an ant were as big as a person, she could lift a car.
challenging.who: A common idea in cartoons and quiz books
challenging.for: An ant can carry a load heavier than her own body. So a person-sized ant sounds as if she could lift something very heavy.
challenging.against: When a body gets bigger, the weight grows much faster than the strength. A person-sized ant would be very heavy, and would struggle even to hold up her own body. She would not lift a car.
challenging.context: This card is about what would happen to an ant's strength if she grew huge.

challenging.claim: Cut an earthworm in two, and you get two worms.
challenging.for: Some earthworms can grow back a lost tail end, so a worm with a missing tail can live on.
challenging.against: In most earthworms, the back half dies. The front half, with the mouth and the important parts inside, can sometimes grow a new tail. So you do not get two worms. And cutting harms the worm, so never cut one.
challenging.context: This card is about a belief that is wrong, and unkind to try.

challenging.claim: Insects are like little machines. They only react, and cannot learn.
challenging.who: Albrecht Bethe, a German scientist, in 1898, and others after him
challenging.for: Many insect actions are the same every time, and are built into the body from birth. A newly hatched ant knows how to walk and clean herself without being taught.
challenging.against: Charles Henry Turner showed in 1907 that ants learn their way home, and later that bees learn colours. Bees also learn to tell their sisters where food is, and bumblebees can learn to pull a string to get food.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument: how much do insects learn and think?

big_questions.q: If an ant grew as big as a dog, could she still carry a crumb bigger than her head?
big_questions.hint: Think about the crumb test. Then think: when a body gets bigger, which grows faster, the weight or the strength?

big_questions.q: Why do insects have six legs, not two or four?
big_questions.hint: Watch an ant walk. Many insects keep three legs on the ground at a time, in a triangle, like a stool with three legs. Can a stool with three legs fall over?

big_questions.q: An earthworm has no eyes, but moves away from light. How can a body sense light without eyes?
big_questions.hint: Close your eyes and stand in the sun. Can your skin tell where the Sun is?

big_questions.q: A bee sees colours on a flower that you cannot see. Is the colour in the flower, or in the eyes looking at the flower?
big_questions.hint: A bee sees ultraviolet patterns on many flowers. A person sees no pattern there. Who is seeing the real flower?

big_questions.q: There are far more ants on Earth than people. Whose planet is it?
big_questions.hint: Scientists guess there are about two and a half million ants for every person on Earth.

story.title: The Crumb That Walked
story.note: A made-up story. The facts in it are true: ants carry crumbs bigger than their heads, spiders have eight legs, and plain tiger butterflies, like many other butterflies, hold their two small front legs folded up.
text: Meenakshi lived on the fourth floor of a building in Chennai. She was seven. Her brother Arjun was five. Their grandmother, Paati, lived with them.
One evening after dinner, Meenakshi was sweeping the kitchen floor. She stopped. A white crumb was moving across the floor, all by itself.
'Arjun!' she called. 'Come and see. The crumb is walking!'
Arjun ran in and squatted down. 'Crumbs cannot walk,' he said. Then he looked closer. 'There is an ant underneath!'
The ant was tiny and black. She held the crumb up in her jaws and walked fast, as if the crumb weighed nothing. The crumb was bigger than her whole head.

Paati came in with her reading glasses on. She bent down and watched. 'That crumb is from your biscuit,' she said. 'She is taking it home to her nest. Look, there is the line of her sisters, going under the door.'
'How do you know they are sisters?' asked Arjun.
'Nearly all the ants in a nest are sisters,' said Paati. 'They have one mother, the queen. She stays in the nest and lays the eggs. Her daughters do all the work.'
Meenakshi fetched the magnifying glass from Paati's sewing box. She held the glass over the ant line. The ants grew big and shiny.
'Let me count her legs,' she said. 'One, two, three on this side. One, two, three on that side. Six legs!'
'And two feelers on her head,' said Arjun. 'They are waving.'
'Those are her antennae,' said Paati. 'She smells with them. Every insect has six legs and two antennae.'
Arjun jumped up. 'Let's count another creature. Come!' He ran to the bathroom and pointed at the corner of the ceiling. A spider with long, thin legs hung there, very still, in a messy web.
Meenakshi stood on the step stool and looked through the glass, without touching. She counted slowly. 'One, two, three, four on this side. One, two, three, four on the other side. That is eight!'
'Eight?' said Arjun. 'But insects have six.'
'So the spider is not an insect,' said Meenakshi. She counted again, to be sure. Still eight. 'And look. Her body is in two parts, not three. And she has no antennae.'
'Spiders are spiders,' said Paati. 'They have their own group, with scorpions. That spider has lived in our bathroom for weeks. She catches mosquitoes in her web.'
Arjun looked up at the spider with new respect. 'Thank you, spider,' he said.
The next morning, the children went out to the balcony. Paati grew pink nithyakalyani flowers in an old paint tin. A big orange butterfly with black edges and white spots was sitting on a flower.
'That is a plain tiger butterfly,' said Paati. 'Watch her drink.' The butterfly uncurled a long, thin tongue, like a straw, and pushed it into the flower.
'Six legs?' asked Arjun.
Meenakshi crept close and held her breath. 'I can see four legs holding on to the flower,' she whispered. 'Only four.'
'Look near her head,' said Paati.
Meenakshi looked hard. There, folded up under the butterfly's head, were two tiny legs, like little arms. 'Six!' she said. 'She keeps two folded up.'
'Many butterflies do that,' said Paati. 'They walk on four legs, but they still have six. That is why we look twice.'
The butterfly opened her wings and flew away over the street.
That afternoon it rained hard. When it stopped, Paati took the children down to the building's garden. On the wet path were three long, pink-brown earthworms.
Arjun bent down. 'How many legs does a worm have?'
Meenakshi looked through the glass. She saw rings all along the worm's body, but no legs at all. 'None,' she said. 'Zero legs.'
'Then how does the worm move?' asked Arjun.
They watched. The worm's front end grew long and thin and pushed forward. Then the body bunched up, short and fat, and the back end slid along.
'Like squeezing toothpaste,' said Meenakshi.
Paati gently moved the worms onto the soil with a leaf, so that nobody would step on them.
That night, Meenakshi drew three pictures in her notebook: an ant with six legs, a spider with eight, and a worm with none. But she kept thinking about the walking crumb.
'Paati,' she said, 'the crumb was bigger than the ant's head. How can she carry something so big?'
Paati smiled. 'Could you carry a sack of rice as big as you?'
Meenakshi thought about the big rice sack in the kitchen. She could not even drag it. 'No,' she said.
'So how big a crumb can an ant carry?' asked Paati. 'Do you think she could carry any crumb at all?'
Meenakshi looked at the biscuit tin. 'I don't know,' she said. 'But I can find out.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: Meenakshi learns to sort small creatures by counting carefully: six legs for an insect, eight for a spider, none for a worm. Counting twice, and looking closely at the butterfly's folded legs, teaches her not to trust a first look. The story ends on a real question the crumb test will answer: how big a load can an ant carry?
ask: How did Meenakshi find out that the spider is not an insect?
Why did the butterfly seem to have only four legs?
How does an earthworm move without legs?

experiments.title: The Crumb Test: how big a crumb can an ant carry?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put biscuit crumbs of four sizes beside a line of ants. You watch for 20 minutes. Then you count which crumbs the ants carried away, and how they did it.
experiments.question: Which sizes of crumb can ants carry away, and which are too big?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which crumbs will the ants carry away: the tiny ones, the rice-sized ones, the chana-sized ones, or even the big ones? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All the crumbs come from the same biscuit, so they taste the same. There are 5 crumbs of each size, because one crumb can be luck. All 20 crumbs go in one line, with the sizes mixed up, so every size is the same distance from the ants. We count at 10 minutes and again at 20 minutes.
results_table: How the ants moved them: one ant, a team, or bit by bit

materials.item: one plain sweet biscuit
a sheet of white paper, or a white plate
a spoon, to break the biscuit
a few grains of sugar, to lead the ants to the paper
a magnifying glass, or a phone camera zoomed in
a pencil and paper for the results, and a clock or phone timer

experiments.safety: Some red ants bite or sting. Watch the ants, but do not touch them or put your hand in the ant line. When you finish, wipe the place with a damp cloth so the ants go home. Do not spray or squash them.

schedule.what: Find an ant line, make 20 crumbs of four sizes, lay them beside the line, watch for 20 minutes, then count and talk.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. A grown-up can write the numbers while your child counts.

setup.art: A spoon breaking a biscuit on a plate into four little heaps: tiny crumbs like sugar grains, crumbs like rice grains, crumbs like chana, and big pieces like a thumbnail.
setup.caption: 1. Break a biscuit into crumbs of four sizes, 5 of each.

setup.art: A white paper on a kitchen floor next to a line of ants, with a pencil line across the paper and 20 crumbs of mixed sizes along it.
setup.caption: 2. Put the 20 crumbs in one line on white paper, sizes mixed, beside the ants.

setup.art: Close-up of tiny ants on the paper: one ant carrying a small crumb, three ants pulling a rice-sized crumb, and many ants crowded on a big crumb.
setup.caption: 3. Watch for 20 minutes. Which crumbs move, and how?

setup.art: A child counting the crumbs left on the paper, with a results table beside her showing the four sizes.
setup.caption: 4. Count the crumbs left of each size.

flow.do: 1. Find a line of ants in the kitchen, on the balcony or by a window. 2. Look at the ants with the magnifying glass. 3. Count the legs on one ant.
flow.say: Let's find some ants. Look at one through the glass. How many legs does she have? How big is her head?
flow.kid: Find a line of ants. Look at one through the glass. Count her legs.
flow.parent: If you cannot find ants, put a pinch of sugar on a plate on the kitchen platform. Look again after an hour. In most Indian homes, ants come within a few hours. If none come, try again the next day.

flow.do: 1. Break the biscuit with the spoon. 2. Make 5 tiny crumbs, the size of sugar grains. 3. Make 5 crumbs the size of rice grains. 4. Make 5 crumbs the size of a chana. 5. Make 5 big pieces, the size of your thumbnail.
flow.say: We need four sizes of crumb. Five tiny ones, five like rice, five like chana and five as big as your thumbnail.
flow.kid: Make 5 crumbs of each size. Tiny, rice, chana and thumbnail.
flow.parent: The sizes do not need to be exact. What matters is four clearly different sizes, with the smallest about as small as a sugar grain.

flow.do: Ask your child which crumbs the ants will carry away, and why. Write the guess down.
flow.say: The ants will find these crumbs soon. Which sizes do you think they will carry away? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which crumbs will the ants carry away? Why?

good: Only the tiny ones, because ants are tiny.
The rice ones too, because I saw an ant carry a big crumb.
None of the big ones, because they are heavier than an ant.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine, as long as there is a reason. Do not tell your child what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Draw a pencil line across the paper, two fingers from one edge. 2. Put the 20 crumbs along the line, mixing the sizes. 3. Put the paper next to the ant line, with the pencil line nearest the ants. 4. Drop a few sugar grains between the ants and the paper.
flow.say: Let's mix up the sizes along the line, so every size is just as close to the ants. Now we put the paper beside the ants.
flow.kid: Put the crumbs along the line. Mix the sizes. Put the paper by the ants.
flow.parent: The sugar grains lead the ants onto the paper. If no ant has reached the paper after 10 minutes, move the paper so that it touches the ant line.

flow.do: 1. Start the timer. 2. Watch quietly for 10 minutes. 3. Count the crumbs left of each size and write them down.
flow.say: Let's watch quietly for ten minutes. Which crumbs are moving? Is one ant carrying, or many ants together?
flow.kid: Watch the crumbs. Which ones move? One ant, or many?

ask.q: What are the ants doing with the big crumbs?
good: Lots of ants are standing on them.
They are biting bits off.
Three ants are pulling one together.

flow.parent: Usually the tiny crumbs go first, each carried by one ant. Rice-sized crumbs are carried by one big ant, or pulled by a team of small ants. Chana-sized and thumbnail crumbs are usually too big to move. The ants crowd on them and bite off small bits. Different kinds of ants act differently, so your results may differ.

flow.do: Watch for 10 more minutes. After 20 minutes in all, count the crumbs left of each size again and write them down.
flow.say: Ten more minutes. Which crumbs are moving now? Then we count again.
flow.kid: Watch ten more minutes. Then count again. How many of each size are left?

flow.do: Ask what your child thinks, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Which crumbs did the ants carry? Was your guess right? Did any ant carry a crumb bigger than her own head?
flow.kid: Which crumbs went? Did an ant carry a crumb bigger than her head?

ask.q: Why did the big crumbs stay?
good: They were too heavy for the ants.
The ants ate them in little bits instead.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the numbers: 'All 5 tiny crumbs went, 2 rice crumbs went, and no big pieces moved.' Different ants give different results, and that is fine. Now read the card on why small bodies are strong for their size.

experiments.title: Damp or Dry: where does an earthworm go? (if you can get earthworms)
experiments.context: In this experiment you give earthworms a choice between damp paper and dry paper, under a cover. After 10 minutes, you look where they went. Do this only if you can find earthworms after rain, or get them from a plant nursery that sells vermicompost.
experiments.question: If an earthworm can choose, will they go to damp paper or dry paper?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the worms go to the damp side, the dry side, or stay in the middle? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both sides are the same paper and the same size. Both are covered, so both are equally dark. Only one thing is different: one side is damp. We use 3 or more worms, because one worm could go either way by chance.

materials.item: 3 to 5 earthworms, found on a path after rain or from a nursery that sells vermicompost
a steel plate or a tray
two pieces of paper towel or newspaper
a little water
a cloth or a second plate to cover the tray

experiments.safety: Wash your hands with soap after touching soil and worms. Handle the worms gently, with wet hands or a leaf, and put them back in the soil afterwards.

schedule.what: Set up a damp side and a dry side, put the worms in the middle, cover, wait 10 minutes and look.

experiments.record: Draw the tray, the damp side and the dry side, and where each worm was after 10 minutes.

setup.art: A steel tray with a damp dark paper towel on the left half and a dry pale paper towel on the right half.
setup.caption: 1. Make one side damp and one side dry.

setup.art: Three earthworms lying across the middle line of the tray, between the damp and dry paper.
setup.caption: 2. Lay the worms gently on the middle line.

setup.art: The tray covered with a cloth, and a phone timer showing 10 minutes.
setup.caption: 3. Cover the tray and wait 10 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Put two paper towels side by side on the tray. 2. Sprinkle water on one, until damp but not dripping. 3. Leave the other dry.
flow.say: One side is damp and one is dry. Everything else is the same.
flow.kid: Make one side damp. Keep the other side dry.
flow.parent: A grown-up should help collect and hold the worms. Wet your hands first, because dry hands can harm a worm's skin.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess where the worms will go, and why.
flow.say: Where do you think the worms will go? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Damp side or dry side? Why?

good: The damp side, because worms live in wet soil.
The dry side, because worms come out when it rains.

flow.do: 1. Lay the worms gently across the middle line. 2. Cover the tray. 3. Wait 10 minutes. 4. Lift the cover and see where each worm is.
flow.say: Let's cover them, so it is dark on both sides. In ten minutes we will look.
flow.kid: Cover the tray. Wait ten minutes. Then look.
flow.parent: Most worms usually move to the damp side. An earthworm breathes through the skin, and the skin must stay damp to do that. If the worms stay in the middle or go to the dry side, write that down too. Worms sometimes do not move much.

check.q: Why do earthworms choose damp places?
options: They breathe through their skin, and the skin must stay damp
They like the colour of damp paper
check.why: An earthworm breathes through the skin, which only works when the skin is damp. If you chose warmth, remember that both sides were in the same room and under the same cover.

flow.do: Put the worms back on damp soil, in a pot or in the garden. Wash hands.
flow.say: Thank you, worms. Let's put them back in the soil, where they live.
flow.kid: Put the worms back in the soil. Wash your hands.

activities.title: Who Shares Our Flat? A small creature hunt
activities.context: In this activity you search your home for small creatures for 10 minutes. For each one you find, you count the legs from a safe distance, and decide: insect, spider, or something else?

materials.item: a torch
a magnifying glass, or a phone camera zoomed in
a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: Look, but do not touch. Some ants bite, and wasps and bees can sting. Never put your fingers into cracks or behind heavy furniture.

schedule.what: Hunt for small creatures for 10 minutes, count legs, and sort what you found.

activities.record: A table with three columns: the creature, the number of legs, and insect, spider or other.

setup.art: A child with a torch looking into the top corner of a bathroom, where a thin-legged spider hangs in a web.
setup.caption: 1. Look in corners, near lights, by windows and in the kitchen.

setup.art: A notebook table with drawings: an ant with 6 legs, a spider with 8 legs, a mosquito with 6 legs, and the words insect, spider, insect.
setup.caption: 2. Count the legs and write what you found.

flow.do: Tell your child where small creatures often hide: ceiling corners, near lights, window frames, the kitchen platform, under the sink.
flow.say: Small creatures live in every home. Let's find as many as we can in ten minutes. Where should we look first?
flow.kid: Small creatures live in every home. Where will you look first?
flow.parent: Ants and spiders are found in almost every home. You may also find a mosquito, a housefly, a moth near a light, a silverfish behind books, or a cockroach.

flow.do: Hunt together. For each creature, count the legs from a safe distance with the glass or the phone zoom. Write or draw each one.
flow.say: Found one! Let's count the legs without touching. How many on each side?
flow.kid: Count the legs. How many on each side? Write it down.

ask.q: Is it easier to count one side at a time?
good: Yes. Three on one side and three on the other make six.
Yes, I counted four and four, so eight.

flow.parent: Moving legs are hard to count. A phone photo, zoomed in, makes it much easier.

flow.do: Sort your list into insects (six legs), spiders (eight legs) and others.
flow.say: Which ones are insects? Which ones are spiders? Were there any with no legs, or lots of legs?
flow.kid: Sort your list. Six legs, eight legs, or other?

activities.title: Build an Insect and a Spider from Dough
activities.context: In this activity you make a model ant and a model spider from atta dough and broom sticks. Making them shows you the difference: how many body parts, how many legs, and where the legs join.

materials.item: a lump of atta dough, or clay, about the size of a lemon
14 short pieces of broom stick or toothpick, for legs (6 for the ant, 8 for the spider)
2 more short pieces, for the ant's antennae
a steel plate to build on

activities.safety: A grown-up breaks the sticks, because the ends can be sharp. If you use matchsticks, break off the heads first.

schedule.what: Make an ant with three body parts and six legs, and a spider with two body parts and eight legs. Compare them.

activities.record: Draw your two models, and label the legs and body parts.

setup.art: Three small balls of dough in a row on a steel plate: head, thorax and abdomen, with six sticks pushed into the middle ball and two short sticks in the head.
setup.caption: 1. Make an ant: three balls, six legs in the middle ball, two antennae.

setup.art: Two balls of dough on a steel plate, with eight sticks pushed into the front ball, four on each side.
setup.caption: 2. Make a spider: two balls, eight legs in the front ball.

flow.do: 1. Roll three small balls of dough for the ant: a head, a middle and a bigger back part. 2. Press them together in a row. 3. Push three legs into each side of the middle ball. 4. Push two antennae into the head.
flow.say: An ant has three body parts. All six legs go into the middle part. Where do the antennae go?
flow.kid: Make three balls. Six legs go in the middle ball. Two antennae on the head.
flow.parent: Children often put legs on all three parts. Let them, then ask them to check the ant in the kitchen, or the drawing on the card 'What makes an insect': where do the legs join?

flow.do: 1. Roll two balls for the spider: a front part and a round back part. 2. Push four legs into each side of the front ball. 3. Add no antennae.
flow.say: A spider has two body parts. Eight legs go into the front part. Does a spider have antennae?
flow.kid: Make two balls. Eight legs go in the front ball. No antennae.

flow.do: Put the two models side by side and compare.
flow.say: Look at the ant and the spider. What is different? What is the same?
flow.kid: Look at both. What is different? What is the same?

good: The ant has six legs and the spider has eight.
The ant has three parts and the spider has two.
Only the ant has antennae.

check.q: On an insect, where do all six legs join the body?
check.why: All six legs join the thorax, the middle part. The head has the eyes, mouth and antennae.

activities.title: If I Were an Ant: draw a load my size
activities.context: In this activity you compare your body with an ant's. You draw round your child on newspaper. Then you draw a crumb next to the outline, bigger than the head, like the ant's crumb.

materials.item: old newspapers, taped together to be as long as your child
a crayon or sketch pen
cello tape

schedule.what: Draw round your child on newspaper, then draw a crumb as big, for them, as the ant's crumb was for the ant.

activities.record: A photo or a small drawing of your outline and your giant crumb.

setup.art: A child lying on taped newspapers on the floor while a grown-up draws round her with a crayon.
setup.caption: 1. Lie on the newspaper. A grown-up draws round you.

setup.art: The child's outline on the newspaper, and next to the head a big circle drawn larger than the head, labelled 'my crumb'.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a crumb bigger than your head, like the ant's.

flow.do: 1. Tape the newspapers together on the floor. 2. Your child lies on them. 3. Draw round your child's body.
flow.say: Lie still. I am drawing round you, so we can see how big you are.
flow.kid: Lie still on the paper. Your grown-up draws round you.

flow.do: Draw a crumb next to your child's outline, bigger than their head. Say that an ant can carry a crumb bigger than her own head.
flow.say: An ant can carry a crumb bigger than her own head. Here is a crumb bigger than your head.
flow.kid: Draw a crumb bigger than your head. That is your ant crumb.

flow.do: Talk about carrying a load as heavy as your child.
flow.say: A big sack of rice weighs about as much as you. An ant can carry a load heavier than herself. Could you pick up a sack as heavy as you and run home with it?
flow.kid: Could you carry a load as heavy as you are? Why not?

ask.q: Why can an ant carry so much for her size?
good: Because she is small and light.
Because her body does not weigh much.

flow.parent: A 25 kg rice sack weighs about as much as a child in Class 2. Many ants can carry more than their own weight. This is the idea on the card 'Small bodies are strong for their size'.
flow.think: Is the ant strong, or is the ant small? Or both?

activities.title: Butterfly Watch (if a butterfly visits your balcony or a park nearby)
activities.context: In this activity you watch a butterfly drinking from a flower. You count her legs, look for her long tongue and see how she holds her wings.

materials.item: a flowering plant on a balcony, or flowers in a park
a phone camera, or a notebook and pencil

schedule.what: Wait quietly near flowers in the late morning, watch a butterfly, and count her legs.

activities.record: A drawing of the butterfly, showing her legs, antennae and tongue.

setup.art: A child sitting very still on a balcony next to a pot of flowering plants, with a butterfly on a flower.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still near flowers, about two big steps away.

setup.art: Close-up of a butterfly drinking from a flower with her long curled tongue, showing four legs holding on and two tiny legs folded under the head.
setup.caption: 2. Look for her tongue, and count her legs.

flow.do: Sit about two big steps from the flowers, in the late morning when butterflies are busy. Keep still and quiet.
flow.say: Butterflies fly away from quick moves. Let's sit like statues and wait.
flow.kid: Sit very still near the flowers. Wait for a butterfly.
flow.parent: Butterflies like sunny, warm places with flowers such as ixora, lantana or nithyakalyani. If none comes in 10 minutes, try another day, or visit a park.

flow.do: When a butterfly lands, count her legs, look for her long tongue and look at her antennae. Take a photo if you can.
flow.say: How many legs can you see holding on? Look near her head too. Can you see her tongue going into the flower?
flow.kid: Count her legs. Look near her head. Find her long tongue.
flow.parent: Many butterflies, like the plain tiger and the common crow, hold their two small front legs folded up. They seem to have four legs. A photo zoomed in shows all six.

printables.title: 4 mats to lay on the floor

rules: Lay the four mats on the floor, a little apart.
Mix the cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns to be the card turner. The card turner turns over the top card and reads the name aloud.
Everyone, including the card turner, races to put one hand on the mat they think is right. A hand on the wrong mat means you sit out that card.
The card turner reads the back aloud to check. The first hand on the right mat wins the card. If nobody was right, put the card at the bottom of the pile.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most cards wins. If two players have the same number, they both win.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards and the 4 mats. 2. Lay the four mats on the floor and mix the cards into a face-down pile.
flow.say: Here are sixteen small creatures. Each one has six legs, eight legs, no legs or lots of legs. Let's lay out the mats.
flow.kid: Lay the four mats on the floor. Mix the cards.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to turn over a card and read the name. 2. Everyone races to the right mat. 3. Read the back aloud.
flow.say: Scorpion! Six, eight, none or lots? Quick!
flow.kid: Turn over a card. Slap the right mat. Read the back.

ask.q: A butterfly seems to stand on four legs. Which mat does she go on?
good: Six legs, because she keeps two folded up.
Six, because a butterfly is an insect.

flow.parent: The tricky cards are the butterfly, the scorpion and the centipede. Let the children argue, then read the back.

flow.do: Count the cards on each mat together.
flow.say: Which mat has the most cards? Why do you think there are so many insects?
flow.kid: Which mat has the most cards?
flow.parent: There are more kinds of insects than of any other animal group. Scientists have named about a million kinds.

games.title: Bee Dance: find the hidden flower
games.context: A honeybee who finds flowers flies home and dances. Her dance tells her sisters which way to fly, and how far. In this game, one player hides a 'flower' and dances to show the others where to find it.

setup.art: A child hiding a paper flower under a cushion while two others cover their eyes.
setup.caption: 1. The dancer hides the paper flower.

setup.art: The child walking a few steps towards the sofa while waggling her body from side to side, and the others watching.
setup.caption: 2. The dancer waggles towards the flower. Long waggle means far.

printables.title: 8 hiding cards to cut out
items: Hide the flower near the front door.
Hide the flower under a cushion.
Hide the flower near the kitchen sink.
Hide the flower on a bookshelf.
Hide the flower near a window.
Hide the flower behind a curtain.
Hide the flower near your bed.
Hide the flower on a chair.

printables.title: 1 paper flower to cut out and colour

rules: The first dancer takes a hiding card, hides the paper flower in that place, and the others close their eyes.
The dancer stands in the middle of the room. No talking!
The dancer waggles their body from side to side while walking towards the flower, then walks back to the middle. They do this three times.
A short waggle walk of two or three steps means the flower is near. A long waggle walk of many steps means the flower is far.
The other players follow the dance and search. The first to find the flower is the next dancer.
Play until everyone has been the dancer once. With two players, the finder always becomes the dancer, so you take turns.

flow.do: Tell the children how real honeybees dance.
flow.say: A bee who finds flowers flies home and dances on the honeycomb. She waggles as she walks. The direction tells her sisters which way to go. A longer waggle means the flowers are further away.
flow.kid: Bees dance to show the way to flowers. A long waggle means far away.

flow.do: Play several rounds. Each time, the dancer hides the flower and dances, without talking.
flow.say: No words! Only the dance. Which way is the dancer pointing? Is the waggle walk long or short?
flow.kid: Watch the dance. Which way? Near or far? Go and find the flower!
flow.parent: Real bees dance on the honeycomb in the dark hive. The direction of the waggle walk shows which way to fly, and the length shows how far. In the game, the dancer simply walks towards the flower.

flow.do: Talk about what the game shows.
flow.say: Was it easy to find the flower from a dance? How do you think the bee sisters learn to read the dance?
flow.kid: Was the dance easy to follow? How do bees learn it?

projects.title: Small Creature Diary: one window, five days
projects.context: In this project you watch one place in your home for five minutes every day for five days: a window sill, a balcony corner or the kitchen platform. You write down every small creature you see, with their legs counted.

materials.item: a notebook with a page for each day
a pencil, and a magnifying glass or a phone camera

schedule.what: Choose the place. Watch for 5 minutes. Draw each creature you see, count the legs and make a tally mark for each.
Watch the same place at the same time. Add any new creatures.
Watch again. Which creature has the most tally marks so far?
Watch again. Did the weather change what you saw?
Watch for the last time. Then count up: how many insects, how many spiders, how many others?

projects.record: The five-day diary, with a final tally of insects, spiders and others.

setup.art: A window sill with a potted plant, an ant walking along the edge and a small spider in the corner of the frame.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one place to watch every day.

setup.art: A notebook page with tally marks next to small drawings of an ant, a spider and a fly.
setup.caption: 2. Make a tally mark for each creature you see.

flow.do: Choose the place with your child. Watch for 5 minutes. Your child draws each creature, counts the legs and makes a tally mark for each one.
flow.say: This is our watching place for five days. Let's see who visits. Draw each one and count their legs.
flow.kid: This is your watching place. Draw who you see. Count their legs.

flow.do: On days 2, 3 and 4, watch the same place at about the same time, for 5 minutes. Add tally marks. On day 4, also look at the weather and write whether it changed who came.
flow.say: Same place, same time. Who is here today? Is anyone new?
flow.kid: Watch the same place. Who is here today? Make tally marks.
flow.wait: Do this once a day, on days 2, 3 and 4.
flow.parent: Watching at the same time each day is fairer, because different creatures come out at different times.

flow.do: On day 5, watch for 5 minutes, then count up all the tally marks.
flow.say: Let's count. How many insects did you see? How many spiders? Which creature came every day?
flow.kid: Count your marks. Who came most often?

ask.q: Which creature did you see most often? Why might that be?
good: Ants, because they live in the wall nearby.
Mosquitoes, because they come in the evening.

challenges.title: Web Builder: make a web that catches the most paper flies
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A spider builds a web of silk to catch flying insects. Now you build a web of thread on a clothes hanger, and test how many paper 'flies' it catches.
challenges.problem: Can you build a thread web on a clothes hanger that catches some of the 10 paper balls thrown at it? Count the catches, change one thing, and try to catch more.
constraints: Use one clothes hanger and one reel of sewing thread, or wool.
Use cello tape to make the threads sticky, but no paper or cloth in the middle of the web.
The paper flies are 10 small balls of paper, each about the size of a grape.
Throw each fly gently from three big steps away.
materials: a clothes hanger, wire or plastic
a sheet of newspaper for 10 paper balls
general: Tie threads from side to side across the hanger, like the spokes of a wheel.
Put the threads close together, so the gaps are smaller than a paper ball.
Tie the threads tight, so they do not sag.

Wrap short strips of cello tape round the threads with the sticky side out, like a spider's sticky silk. Plain thread alone will not hold a paper ball. Use light balls of tissue paper if newspaper falls off.
creative: Wind a thread round and round in a spiral over the spokes, like a real spider's web.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own web. Throw 10 paper flies and count how many it catches. Change one thing, then test again. Did it catch more?

setup.art: A plastic clothes hanger with threads tied across it like the spokes of a wheel, and a spiral of thread over them.
setup.caption: 1. Tie threads across the hanger to make a web.

setup.art: A child throwing a small paper ball at the thread web hanging from a door handle, with two balls already caught in the threads.
setup.caption: 2. Throw 10 paper flies and count the catches.

flow.do: Read the challenge together. Look at a real web in a corner if there is one, or at the picture.
flow.say: A spider's web catches flying insects. Can you build a web that catches paper flies?
flow.kid: Build a web. Can it catch paper flies?

flow.do: Your child builds a web on the hanger. Help with knots if needed.
flow.say: Where will you tie the threads? How close together should they be?
flow.kid: Tie threads across the hanger. Make your web.
flow.parent: Let your child try their own idea first, even if the gaps are big. The test will show what works.

flow.do: 1. Hang the web from a door handle. 2. Make 10 paper balls. 3. Throw them gently from three big steps away. 4. Count the catches. 5. Change one thing and test again.
flow.say: Let's test it. How many flies did your web catch? What could you change to catch more?
flow.kid: Throw 10 flies. Count the catches. Change one thing. Try again.

ask.q: What made your web catch more?
good: Putting the threads closer together.
Wrapping more sticky tape round the threads.

check.q: Why does a spider's web catch insects so well?
options: The threads are thin, close together and sticky
The web is made of paper
check.why: A spider's web has many thin threads, close together, and the spiral threads are sticky. An insect who flies in gets stuck. Your web worked better when the gaps were small or the threads were sticky.

worksheets.title: Six Legs, Eight Legs, No Legs (core)

items.p: Look at the drawing of an ant. Count her legs. How many legs does she have?
items.why: An ant has three legs on each side. 3 and 3 make 6. Every insect has six legs.
items.art: A large clear drawing of an ant from above, with three legs on each side.

items.p: Label the ant's body: head, thorax, abdomen, antennae.
a: head: the front part, with the eyes and mouth
thorax: the middle part, where the six legs join
abdomen: the back part, the biggest
antennae: the two feelers on the head
items.why: An insect's body has three parts. The legs join the middle part, the thorax, and the antennae are on the head.
items.art: A big ant from the side with four empty label lines pointing to the head, the middle, the back part and the feelers.

items.p: Sort these small creatures: six legs, or eight legs?
items.why: Ants, honeybees and butterflies are insects, with six legs. Spiders, scorpions and ticks belong to the spider group, with eight legs.
items.art: Six small drawings: an ant, a spider, a honeybee, a scorpion, a butterfly and a tick.

items.p: Remember the crumb test. Draw the four sizes of crumb on the paper, and draw what the ants did with each size.
items.a: Four sizes of crumb. Ants carrying the tiny ones, a team pulling a rice-sized one, and many ants crowded on the big ones.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the four sizes, and shows that the small crumbs were carried away and the big ones were not.
items.art: An empty box for drawing, with a white sheet of paper drawn at the bottom.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: an ant has six legs and a spider has eight. Say one more way a spider's body is different from an ant's.
items.a: A spider's body has two parts, not three, and a spider has no antennae.
items.why: A strong answer says two body parts, or no antennae. It may also say that a spider has no wings.

items.p: A butterfly drinks from a flower with a long, thin tongue, like a straw.
items.why: True. A butterfly uncurls her long tongue and puts the tongue into the flower to drink.

items.p: An earthworm has many tiny legs.
items.why: False. An earthworm has no legs. Tiny stiff bristles on each ring of the body grip the soil, and muscles squeeze and stretch the body.

items.p: Draw a line from each creature to the way they move.
pairs: squeezes and stretches, with no legs
items.why: A butterfly flies, an ant walks on six legs, an earthworm squeezes and stretches, and a snail glides on one foot.
items.art: Four creatures on the left and four ways of moving on the right, mixed up.

items.p: Kavya, aged 7, lives in Kochi. A thin-legged spider has made a web in the corner of her bathroom.

views.says: The spider is scary. Let's sweep the web away.
Leave her there. She catches mosquitoes for us.
Gently move the spider outside on a piece of paper. Then nobody is scared, and she can still catch insects.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing another person has right. Say it out loud, or a grown-up can write it for you.
items.a: A strong answer picks one view and gives a reason. The mother is right that house spiders catch mosquitoes and flies. Kavya is right that her feelings matter. The aunt finds a way that helps both Kavya and the spider.
items.why: Common house spiders are not dangerous and they catch insects. Moving a spider gently, or leaving her, both avoid harming her.

items.p: Ants and honeybees live together in big families called ________.
items.why: A colony is a big family who live together and share the work. In an ant colony, nearly all the ants are sisters.

items.p: Three of these are insects. Which one is not?
items.why: A spider has eight legs and two body parts, so a spider is not an insect. The others all have six legs.

items.p: Draw a spider and an insect side by side. Show the right number of legs and body parts on each.
items.a: An insect with three body parts, six legs on the middle part and two antennae. A spider with two body parts, eight legs on the front part and no antennae.
items.why: A strong drawing gets the legs right (6 and 8), the body parts right (3 and 2), and gives antennae only to the insect.
items.art: An empty box for drawing, split down the middle, with 'Insect' on the left and 'Spider' on the right.

items.p: Every spider builds a web to catch food.
items.why: False. Jumping spiders have no web. They creep up on their food and jump on it.

items.p: Put these small creatures in order, from the fewest legs to the most legs.
items.why: An earthworm has no legs, an ant has six, a spider has eight and a centipede has lots.

items.p: All the worker ants in a colony are female.
items.why: True. The worker ants are sisters, daughters of the queen. Male ants hatch only at some times of year, and do not do the work of the nest.

items.p: Silk is a strong, thin thread made inside an animal's body. Which of these animals makes silk?
items.why: A spider makes silk at the back end of her body, and uses it for her web.

items.p: Label the spider: front part, back part, legs, eyes.
a: front part: where the legs, eyes and mouth are
back part: the round part, where the silk comes out
legs: eight, all joined to the front part
eyes: on the top of the front part, often eight
items.why: A spider's body has two parts. All eight legs join the front part, and the silk comes out of the back part.
items.art: A large drawing of a spider from above with four empty label lines.

items.p: Match each small creature to one job they do.
pairs: carries pollen from flower to flower
turns dead leaves into rich soil
carries away fallen crumbs and dead insects
items.why: Bees carry pollen while they collect food, worms eat dead leaves and soil, spiders catch insects, and ants clear up crumbs and dead insects.
items.art: A bee, an earthworm, a spider and an ant on the left, and four pictures of their jobs on the right, mixed up.

items.p: Fatima, a girl in Hyderabad, says: 'Ants are the strongest animals in the world.' Is she right? Say what you think, and why. (Say it out loud, or a grown-up can write it for you.)
items.a: She is partly right. For their size, ants are very strong: they carry crumbs bigger than their heads. But an elephant can lift a much heavier log than any ant. It depends on whether you compare the size of the load with the size of the animal.
items.why: A strong answer says ants are strong for their size, but not the strongest in total, and explains the difference.

items.p: The two feelers on an insect's head are called ________.
items.why: Antennae are the two feelers on an insect's head. Insects smell and touch with them.

items.p: Lakshmi lives in a flat in Mysuru. A line of ants walks from a crack in the kitchen wall to the sugar tin.

views.says: Draw a chalk line round the tin, or spray the ants. They are in our food.
The ants are only taking crumbs home to their sisters. Let them be.
Close the sugar tin tightly and wipe up the crumbs. The ants will stop coming, and nobody gets hurt.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say what one other person has right. Say it out loud, or a grown-up can write it for you.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and gives a reason. The grandmother is right that food must stay clean. Lakshmi is right that the ants are doing their own work and mean no harm. The mother's way keeps food clean without killing ants, by removing what draws them.
items.why: Ants come where they find food. Closing tins and wiping crumbs works well, and is kinder than spray. Some chalks sold for ants have poison in them, so they must be kept away from children.

items.p: Imagine an ant made as big as a dog. Would she still carry a crumb bigger than her own head? Say why. (Say it out loud, or a grown-up can write it for you.)
items.a: No. When a body gets bigger, the weight grows much faster than the strength of the muscles. A dog-sized ant would be very heavy, and would have little strength left for a load.
items.why: A strong answer says that weight grows faster than strength as a body gets bigger. It may use numbers: twice as big each way means about 4 times the strength but about 8 times the weight.

items.p: Which of these gives the best reason why a small ant can carry a big crumb?
opts: Ants eat a lot of sugar
A small body is very light for the strength of the muscles
Ants have more legs than people
items.why: A small body weighs very little compared with how strong the muscles are, so there is strength left over for a load. Sugar and the number of legs do not explain it.

items.p: Ishaan, a boy in Class 2, did the crumb test with tiny red ants. His big crumbs stayed, but the ants ate them in little bits. His cousin Divya used big black ants, and one ant carried a rice crumb alone. Why were the results different? (Say it out loud, or a grown-up can write it for you.)
items.a: The ants were different kinds and sizes. A big black ant is stronger than a tiny red ant, so she can carry a bigger crumb alone. The tiny ants worked as a team or ate the crumb bit by bit.
items.why: A strong answer says different kinds of ants are different sizes and strengths, so a fair comparison must use the same kind of ant.

items.p: Draw how an earthworm moves, in three pictures: long and thin, then short and fat, then long and thin again, further along.
items.a: Three drawings of a worm. In the second, the body is short and fat. In the third, the front end has moved further forward.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the worm stretching forward, then bunching up and pulling the back along, so the whole worm moves forward.
items.art: An empty box for drawing with three rows.

items.p: Sort these: insect, spider group, or neither?
items.why: Dragonflies and houseflies have six legs, so they are insects. Scorpions and ticks have eight, so they belong to the spider group. Earthworms have no legs, and centipedes have many, so they are neither.
items.art: Six small drawings: a dragonfly, a scorpion, an earthworm, a centipede, a housefly and a tick.

items.p: If an ant grew as big as a person, she could lift a car.
items.why: False. When a body gets bigger, the weight grows much faster than the strength. A person-sized ant would be very heavy and would have little strength left for a load.

items.p: Label the honeybee: antennae, wings, thorax, abdomen, legs.
a: antennae: two feelers on the head
wings: four, joined to the thorax
legs: six, joined to the thorax
items.why: Both the wings and the legs of an insect join the thorax, the middle part. The abdomen is at the back.
items.art: A large honeybee from the side with five empty label lines.

items.p: Three of these live in colonies and share the work. Which one usually lives alone?
items.why: Ants, honeybees and termites live in colonies. Most spiders, like a house spider, live alone and build their own webs.

items.p: Bumblebees in a test rolled small balls again and again, with no food as a reward. Some scientists say this is play. Others are not sure. What do you think? Give a reason. (Say it out loud, or a grown-up can write it for you.)
items.a: Any answer with a reason. For example: 'I think it is play, because they did it again and again with no food.' Or: 'Maybe they were only checking the balls, so I am not sure.'
items.why: A strong answer gives a view and a reason from what the bees did. Scientists still argue about this, so both answers can be strong.

quiz.p: How many legs does every grown-up insect have?
quiz.why: Every grown-up insect has six legs, three on each side. Ants, bees and butterflies all have six.

quiz.p: Which of these is an insect?
quiz.why: A honeybee has six legs, three body parts and two antennae, so she is an insect. A spider has eight legs and an earthworm has none.

quiz.p: Meera, a girl in Pune, counts eight legs on a small creature in a corner. What is the creature?
opts: A spider, or one of the spider group
quiz.why: Eight legs means the spider group. If you picked an insect, remember that insects have six legs.

quiz.p: How many parts does a spider's body have?
quiz.why: A spider's body has two parts: a front part with the legs, and a round back part. An insect's body has three parts.

quiz.p: How does an earthworm move without legs?
opts: The body squeezes and stretches, and tiny bristles grip the soil
The worm rolls like a ball
quiz.why: Muscles make the body long and thin, then short and fat. Tiny bristles on each ring hold on to the soil, so the worm moves forward.

quiz.p: Roshni, a girl in Kolkata, sees a butterfly standing on four legs. What is true?
opts: The butterfly has lost two legs
The butterfly has six legs, but keeps two folded up
quiz.why: Many butterflies keep their two small front legs folded up near the head. They still have six legs.

quiz.p: In the crumb test, what did the ants usually do with the biggest crumbs?
opts: Crowded on them and bit off small bits
quiz.why: The biggest crumbs were too big for one ant to carry, so many ants crowded on them and took small bits home. If you picked 'carried them away', look again at how many big crumbs were left.

quiz.p: Why did we put all the crumbs along one line, with the sizes mixed up?
opts: So every size was the same distance from the ants
So the ants could not find them
quiz.why: Mixing the sizes along one line makes the test fair. No size was closer to the ants than another.

quiz.p: Why can a small ant carry a load bigger than her head, when a person cannot carry a load bigger than the person?
opts: A small body is very light for the strength of the muscles
Ants eat more food than people
quiz.why: A small body weighs very little compared with the strength of the muscles. Ants have no bones inside at all. Their hard skin is on the outside.

quiz.p: What does a honeybee's dance tell her sisters?
opts: Which way to fly, and how far, to find flowers
quiz.why: The waggle dance shows which way to fly and how far. A bee learns where the flowers are, and tells her sisters.

Engineers study how ants share a heavy load, to build small robots that carry things together.
Scientists study spider silk, which is very strong for how thin it is, to make new strong threads.

open_questions.q: Why do earthworms come up out of the soil after rain?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have several ideas. The soil may have too little air when it is full of water. Or the wet ground lets worms travel far without drying out. Nobody is sure which matters most.
Scientists can see what insects do, and that bees seem to play. What being a bee or an ant feels like is still unknown, and scientists argue about it.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of insects are there?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have named about a million kinds. Many more have never been found or named. Guesses for the real number go from about 5 million to many more.

open_questions.q: Why are insects disappearing from some places?
open_questions.why_open: In some countries, scientists have counted fewer insects than before. Loss of wild places, poisons sprayed on crops and changes in weather may all play a part. In many places, including much of India, nobody has counted for long enough to know.

maths.problem: Meenakshi counts the legs on 3 ants. Each ant has 6 legs. How many legs in all?
maths.explain: There are 3 groups of 6 legs. 6 and 6 make 12, and 6 more makes 18.
maths.context: This is about counting legs on insects, as Meenakshi did in the story.
maths.why_maths: Counting in equal groups is quicker than counting every leg one by one.

maths.problem: In the crumb test, 5 tiny crumbs went and 2 rice crumbs went. No chana crumbs or big pieces went. How many crumbs did the ants carry away in all? How many were left, out of 20?
maths.explain: 5 and 2 make 7. There were 20 crumbs at the start. 20 take away 7 is 13.
maths.context: This is about the crumb test, where ants could carry away biscuit crumbs of four sizes.
maths.why_maths: Adding up and taking away shows how much the ants moved, and how much was too big for them.

maths.problem: A spider and an ant stand side by side. The spider has 8 legs and the ant has 6. How many more legs does the spider have? How many legs are there altogether?
maths.answer: The spider has 2 more legs. There are 14 legs altogether.
maths.explain: Count up from 6 to 8: that is 2 more. 8 and 6 make 14.
maths.context: This is about the difference between a spider and an insect.
maths.why_maths: Finding the difference shows clearly how a spider and an insect are not the same.

maths.problem: On a mat there are some ants and some spiders. Altogether there are 20 legs. There is one spider. How many ants are there?
maths.explain: One spider has 8 legs. 20 take away 8 is 12. Each ant has 6 legs, and 6 and 6 make 12. So there are 2 ants.
maths.context: This is a puzzle about counting legs, to tell how many insects there are.
maths.why_maths: If you know how many legs each creature has, you can work backwards from the legs to the creatures.

maths.problem: In the Small Creature Diary, Kavya made these marks over five days. Ants: |||| |||| ||. Spiders: |||. Flies: ||||. Which creature did she see most often, and how many more times than spiders?
maths.answer: Ants, 12 times. That is 9 more times than spiders, who were seen 3 times.
maths.explain: Count each group of tally marks: 5 and 5 and 2 make 12 ants. Spiders have 3 marks. 12 take away 3 is 9.
maths.context: This is about the Small Creature Diary, where you watched one place for five days.
maths.why_maths: Tally marks help you keep count while you watch, and comparing them shows which creature is most common.

roots.context: We have counted legs, met insects, spiders and worms, and watched ants carry crumbs. Now we ask what the crumb test tells us about size, strength and ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: An ant can carry a crumb bigger than her own head. You cannot carry a load as heavy as your own body. A small body weighs very little for the strength of its muscles. So smaller animals are usually stronger for their size.
deep_truth.habit: We think of big as strong and small as weak. But strength depends on size in a surprising way: as a body grows, the weight grows faster than the strength. So a small body is not a weaker copy of a big one. Being small brings its own powers.
deep_truth.evidence: In the crumb test, ants carried the tiny crumbs, and teams sometimes moved bigger ones. In 1638 Galileo worked out that when a body is made bigger, the weight grows faster than the strength.

three.who_am_i: You are a big animal, millions of times heavier than an ant. Your size decides what you can lift, and what you cannot.
three.what_is_life: Life comes in every size. Each size has its own strengths: an ant lifts big loads, and a person can carry a baby a long way.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of small creatures, far more of them than of us. Ants, bees, spiders and worms do huge work together, one small load at a time.

roots.thread: An ant colony carries home far more food than any one ant could. Each ant brings a crumb, and thousands of sisters together feed the whole nest. A honeybee brings home a tiny drop of nectar, and many trips make a comb of honey. Worms move a little soil each, and together they turn over whole fields. The work of one small life joins the work of millions, and the colony, the hive and the soil are what the many build together.

teachings.teaching: This old Jain text says that all beings love their life. They want to be happy and do not want to be hurt. To all of them, life is dear.
teachings.link: An ant who carries a crumb home is working for her own life and her sisters' lives. The Jain teaching asks us to care for the smallest beings, which is why this unit says: watch the ants, but do not spray or squash them.

teachings.teaching: The Bible says: go to the ant and watch her ways. She has no ruler or boss, yet she gathers her food in summer.
teachings.link: In the crumb test, no ant gave orders. Each ant carried what she could, and the colony's food arrived anyway.

teachings.teaching: The Quran tells of an ant who sees King Solomon's army coming. She calls to the other ants to go into their homes, so that they are not crushed.
teachings.link: In this story an ant notices danger, thinks of her sisters and warns them. Real ants also warn and call each other, with smells and touches of their antennae.

science.text: When a body is made bigger, the weight grows faster than the strength. This is why small animals can carry more for their size. Galileo worked this out in 1638.
Bumblebees rolled small balls with no food as a reward, and some scientists think this is play. Whether insects have feelings like ours is still argued about.

other_view.view: An ant carrying a crumb is following ways of acting built into her body from birth. In this view, we should not say that the ant cares about her sisters, or chooses her crumb, the way a person would.

how_we_found_out.story: About 125 years ago, many scientists thought insects were like tiny machines. In 1898, Albrecht Bethe, a German scientist, wrote that ants and bees only react to smells and other signals. He said they cannot learn. Charles Henry Turner, an African American scientist, decided to test this. People were often unfair to Black scientists then, and he did much of his research while teaching in a school. Turner built a small platform with little paths and bridges leading back to an ants' nest. He put ants on the platform and watched them find their way home, again and again. At first they wandered. Then they found their way faster each time, as if they had learned the route. In 1907 he wrote that ants learn and remember the way home. Later he showed that bees learn colours too.
how_we_found_out.who: Charles Henry Turner, an African American scientist and teacher, testing an idea of Albrecht Bethe, a German scientist
how_we_found_out.when: Bethe wrote his idea in 1898. Turner published his ant tests in 1907, and his bee colour tests in 1910.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That insects are like machines, who only react and cannot learn. Turner's tests showed that ants learn their way home and get better with practice.
